newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha raises campaign invective.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha raises campaign invective.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha pushed his party's general election campaign into high gear on Monday, saying his Socialist rivals would meet the same demise as their Communist predecessors who seized power in 1944.

Berisha was addressing an outdoor rally in Tirana after Albania's major parties signed an agreement in Rome pledging to ensure a free and fair ballot on Sunday and recognising the need for a coalition government.

Although Berisha is not up for re-election, he has waged a high-profile campaign to keep intact the large majority his Democratic Party enjoys in parliament. The vote is viewed by many as judgment on his five years in power.

He said the Socialists were linked to "paid gangsters," a reference to self-styled "committees" which still control some southern regions after violence erupted throughout Europe's poorest country in March. Some 1,500 people have died.
"I am warning them they will not enjoy the fruits of victory if they resort to terror or bloodshed," a hoarse Berisha told the cheering crowd, which numbered no more than 700.

"You and your brothers are understandably upset by gang violence. I pledge that on June 29 these gangs will meet an ugly end. We will tell them that like their predecessors in 1944, they will meet the same shameful end."

Albania was ruled by eastern Europe's most repressive Communist regime for 45 years and was one of the last countries in the region to throw off one-party rule. Senior Communists were sentenced to long prison terms and barred from office.
The Socialists, though heirs to the Communist party, say they have been totally reformed and profess free market values.
The Democrats face a tough race after winning all but a handful of the seats in elections a year ago that were criticised as unfair within and outside Albania.
Berisha was forced to call Sunday's early election in March at the height of the rebellion by Albanians who blamed him for the collapse of investment schemes holding their life savings.
He also had to appoint a multi-party government led by the Socialists. A multinational peacekeeping force of 7,000 was dispatched to restore a degree of order.
In Rome, Berisha's Democrats, the Socialists and the Social Democrats signed a "Pact for the Future of Albania" aimed at ensuring a calm atmosphere in the country of 3.4 million.

Socialist leader Fatos Nano pledged to recognise whatever outcome the poll produced but said there was "no possibility" his party would lose. He told reporters that despite intensive monitoring it was still possible that gangs "acting under Berisha's orders" would destroy ballot papers.

Several dozen people have died in the past week and renewed violence claimed at least six more lives in the past 48 hours. The official ATA news agency said three people died in an ambush in Tirana and three more in the central town of Elbasan.
Socialist rallies have tended to draw larger crowds than Berisha's Democrats, but most people at rallies by both sides show little enthusiasm for either candidates or party leaders.

Berisha's pro-market policies initially won U.S. backing after he was first elected by parliament in 1992. But that support ebbed away as he took increasingly authoritarian measures, including his re-election in March a day after the proclamation of a state of emergency.
